nameStory: This tiny speedwell gets its name from its distinctive ivy-shaped leaves, which have the same lobed, angular appearance as English ivy. The "speedwell" part comes from an old farewell blessing meaning "may you prosper" or "Godspeed," given to these plants because they were thought to bring good fortune to travelers.
description: Ivy-leaved speedwell is a small, low-growing annual weed that spreads along the ground in a mat-like pattern. This diminutive plant rarely grows taller than a few inches, with trailing stems that can stretch up to 8 inches long. It produces tiny, delicate blue flowers that are barely visible unless you're looking closely, and its distinctive lobed leaves give it away even when not in bloom.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, distinctly lobed leaves shaped like tiny ivy leaves with 3-5 rounded segments. They feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, growing alternately along the trailing stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Solitary pale blue flowers, each less than half an inch across, tucked individually in leaf joints. The flowers have four petals and are so small you might mistake them for tiny forget-me-nots at first glance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, sprawling mats that hug the ground, with weak stems that trail rather than stand upright. The whole plant has a delicate, almost fragile appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds. The capsules are green initially, turning brown as they mature.

habitat: Look for ivy-leaved speedwell in disturbed soils, garden beds, lawns, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in moist, fertile soil and partial shade, often appearing as a garden weed in flower beds or along pathways. This European immigrant has adapted well to urban and suburban environments.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering, with the distinctive ivy-shaped leaves becoming most noticeable as they spread across bare soil. This is the best time to spot the tiny blue flowers.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering and producing seeds throughout the warmer months, forming more extensive mats in favorable locations. The soft leaves remain the most reliable identifying feature.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline as temperatures drop, with seed capsules maturing and releasing their contents for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely in harsh New England winters, surviving only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Despite producing flowers with both male and female parts, ivy-leaved speedwell is primarily a "selfer" - it pollinates itself before the flowers even fully open, ensuring reproduction even when pollinators are scarce!
confusionNotes: The ivy-shaped leaves make this speedwell fairly distinctive, but it might be confused with small ivy seedlings. Remember: ivy-leaved speedwell has tiny blue flowers and much softer, more delicate leaves, while true ivy has tougher, waxy leaves and never produces blue flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this plant is completely unrelated to English ivy despite the similar leaf shape. It's actually in the plantain family and is much more closely related to snapdragons than to any ivy species.
compareHints: Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves. Most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves - bird's-eye speedwell has round leaves, thyme-leaved speedwell has oval leaves, and corn speedwell has toothed but not lobed leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
